cards.front: State the formula for the area of a parallelogram. What does 'height' mean here?
cards.back: Area of parallelogram = base (b) × height (h). The HEIGHT is the PERPENDICULAR distance between the two parallel sides (the base and its opposite side). It is NOT the slant side. The slant side is used only for the perimeter. Perimeter of parallelogram = 2(a + b), where a and b are adjacent sides.
cards.memory_hook: PARALLELOGRAM AREA: imagine pushing a rectangle sideways — it leans but the SAME area stays (base × perpendicular height). The slant is for perimeter only. BASE × PERPENDICULAR = AREA every time!

cards.front: What is the formula for the area of a triangle? How does it relate to the parallelogram?
cards.back: Area of triangle = ½ × base × height. Relationship: a diagonal of a parallelogram divides it into two EQUAL triangles. Each triangle has exactly HALF the area of the parallelogram. So: Triangle area = ½ × (Parallelogram area) = ½ × base × height. The height is the perpendicular distance from the base to the opposite vertex.
cards.memory_hook: TRIANGLE = HALF a PARALLELOGRAM. Draw a diagonal in ANY parallelogram — two equal triangles appear! Each gets half. So triangle area = ½ × b × h. Remember: ½ is the magic fraction that makes triangles.

cards.front: State the formula for circumference and area of a circle.
cards.back: Circumference (perimeter of circle) = 2πr = πd, where r = radius, d = diameter. Area of circle = πr². π ≈ 22/7 (use when r is a multiple of 7) or π ≈ 3.14 (otherwise). Example: radius = 7 cm → Circumference = 2 × 22/7 × 7 = 44 cm; Area = 22/7 × 7² = 22/7 × 49 = 154 cm².
cards.memory_hook: C = 2πr (go AROUND twice the radius, π times). Area = πr² (SQUARE the radius, multiply by π). Trick: Circumference has the word 'ROUND' in it — 2πr goes ROUND. Area gets SQUARED — πr²!

cards.front: What is π (pi)? What are its two commonly used approximations?
cards.back: π (pi) is the mathematical constant equal to the ratio of any circle's circumference to its diameter: π = C/d. It is an irrational number — it never ends and never repeats: π = 3.14159265... Two approximations used in Class 7: (1) π ≈ 22/7 — use when the radius is a multiple of 7 (e.g., 7, 14, 21, 35 cm); (2) π ≈ 3.14 — use otherwise.
cards.memory_hook: π = C/d = the constant ratio of EVERY circle's circumference to its diameter. Pi day is March 14 (3/14) because π ≈ 3.14! Use 22/7 for multiples of 7 (clean division), use 3.14 for everything else.

cards.front: What is the unit conversion between m² and cm²? Between km² and m²?
cards.back: 1 m = 100 cm, so 1 m² = 100 × 100 = 10,000 cm². To convert m² to cm²: multiply by 10,000. To convert cm² to m²: divide by 10,000. 1 km = 1000 m, so 1 km² = 1000 × 1000 = 1,000,000 m² = 10⁶ m². 1 hectare = 10,000 m² = 100 m × 100 m. 1 km² = 100 hectares.
cards.memory_hook: UNIT SQUARE RULE: if 1 m = 100 cm, then 1 m² = 100² = 10,000 cm². ALWAYS SQUARE the conversion factor! Same for km: 1 km = 1000 m → 1 km² = 1000² = 1,000,000 m². Square the number, square the result!

cards.front: How do you find the area of a path surrounding a rectangle?
cards.back: Steps: (1) Note the inner rectangle dimensions (l × b) and path width (w). (2) Outer length = l + 2w (path adds w on each end). (3) Outer width = b + 2w. (4) Outer area = (l+2w) × (b+2w). (5) Inner area = l × b. (6) Path area = Outer area − Inner area. KEY: the path width is added on BOTH sides (left+right for length; top+bottom for width), so total addition = 2w for each dimension.
cards.memory_hook: PATH adds to BOTH SIDES: +w on left +w on right = +2w total. Like adding a frame to a picture — the frame adds on ALL four sides. Outer = Inner + 2w (each dimension). Path area = Outer − Inner.

cards.front: Why is the height in a parallelogram's area formula the perpendicular height, not the slant side?
cards.back: Area represents the SPACE inside a shape. When you 'straighten up' a parallelogram into a rectangle (by cutting a right triangle from one end and moving it to the other), the base remains the same but the height becomes the VERTICAL (perpendicular) distance — NOT the slant side. The slant side is longer than the perpendicular height (it's the hypotenuse of the right triangle cut off). Using the slant side would overestimate the area.
cards.memory_hook: SLANT SIDE vs HEIGHT: slant side = hypotenuse (LONGER). Perpendicular height = the SHORT vertical distance. AREA uses the SHORT one (perpendicular). PERIMETER uses the LONG one (slant side). Never mix them up!

cards.front: Find the circumference and area of a circle with radius = 21 cm. (Use π = 22/7)
cards.back: Radius r = 21 cm. 21 is a multiple of 7, so use π = 22/7. Circumference = 2πr = 2 × (22/7) × 21 = 2 × 22 × 3 = 132 cm. Area = πr² = (22/7) × 21 × 21 = (22/7) × 441 = 22 × 63 = 1386 cm². Answer: Circumference = 132 cm, Area = 1386 cm².
cards.memory_hook: r = 21 = 3 × 7 → use 22/7. 21 ÷ 7 = 3. Circumference: 2 × 22 × 3 = 132. Area: (22/7) × 441 = 22 × 63 = 1386. Whenever r is a multiple of 7, 22/7 simplifies beautifully!

cards.front: A parallelogram has base 18 cm and height 10 cm. A triangle has the same base and height. Compare their areas.
cards.back: Parallelogram area = base × height = 18 × 10 = 180 cm². Triangle area = ½ × base × height = ½ × 18 × 10 = 90 cm². The triangle's area is exactly HALF the parallelogram's area when they share the same base and height. This confirms the relationship: triangle area = ½ × parallelogram area (same base and height).
cards.memory_hook: SAME BASE + SAME HEIGHT: Triangle = ½ × Parallelogram. Always. No exceptions. If parallelogram = 180, triangle = 90. This relationship is the CORE of why triangle area formula has ½!

cards.front: A square field has side 50 m. A 5 m wide path runs outside. Find the path area.
cards.back: Inner square: side = 50 m. Inner area = 50² = 2500 m². Path width = 5 m, so outer side = 50 + 5 + 5 = 60 m. Outer area = 60² = 3600 m². Path area = 3600 − 2500 = 1100 m².
cards.memory_hook: Square with path: outer side = inner side + 2 × path width = 50 + 10 = 60. Path area = 60² − 50² = 3600 − 2500 = 1100 m². The difference of squares formula works here: 60² − 50² = (60+50)(60−50) = 110 × 10 = 1100!

cards.front: Two rectangles have the same area of 36 cm². Do they necessarily have the same perimeter? Give an example.
cards.back: No! Same area does NOT mean same perimeter. Example: Rectangle 1: 9 cm × 4 cm. Area = 36 cm² ✓. Perimeter = 2(9+4) = 26 cm. Rectangle 2: 12 cm × 3 cm. Area = 36 cm² ✓. Perimeter = 2(12+3) = 30 cm. Rectangle 3: 6 cm × 6 cm (square). Area = 36 cm² ✓. Perimeter = 24 cm. All three have the same area but different perimeters. The square has the MINIMUM perimeter for a given area (among rectangles).
cards.memory_hook: AREA = space inside. PERIMETER = boundary length. Same space can have DIFFERENT boundary lengths. A tall thin rectangle has the same area as a short fat one — but very different perimeters. Shape matters, not just size!

cards.front: A wheel has diameter 84 cm. How far does it travel in 100 complete rotations? (π = 22/7)
cards.back: Diameter = 84 cm, so radius = 42 cm. Circumference = πd = (22/7) × 84 = 22 × 12 = 264 cm. In 1 rotation, the wheel travels 264 cm. In 100 rotations: 100 × 264 = 26,400 cm = 264 m. Answer: The wheel travels 264 m in 100 rotations.
cards.memory_hook: WHEEL DISTANCE = circumference × number of rotations. Each rotation = one circumference length of road covered. 100 rotations = 100 × 264 cm = 26,400 cm = 264 m. Bicycles, cars, trains — ALL use this principle!

cards.front: Find the area of a triangle with base 24 cm and height 15 cm.
cards.back: Area of triangle = ½ × base × height = ½ × 24 × 15 = ½ × 360 = 180 cm². Simple steps: multiply base and height first (24 × 15 = 360), then divide by 2 (360 ÷ 2 = 180). Answer: 180 cm². Always double-check that the height given is perpendicular to the base.
cards.memory_hook: ½ × 24 × 15 = 12 × 15 = 180 cm². Shortcut: take HALF of the base first (24÷2 = 12), then multiply by height (12 × 15 = 180). One multiplication instead of two — always halve the easier number first!

cards.front: The circumference of a circle is 44 cm. Find its radius and area. (π = 22/7)
cards.back: C = 2πr = 44. So 2 × (22/7) × r = 44. (44/7) × r = 44. r = 44 × 7/44 = 7 cm. Area = πr² = (22/7) × 7² = (22/7) × 49 = 22 × 7 = 154 cm². Answer: r = 7 cm, Area = 154 cm². Tip: always find radius FIRST from the given measurement, then calculate area.
cards.memory_hook: Circumference given → find r first. C = 2πr → r = C/(2π) = 44/(2 × 22/7) = 44 × 7/44 = 7. Then area = π × 7² = 154. Always work INWARD: circumference → radius → area!

cards.front: A rectangular park 80 m × 60 m has a 4 m wide path inside along its boundary. Find the area of the path.
cards.back: The path is INSIDE the rectangle. Inner dimensions (what's left after the path): length = 80 − 4 − 4 = 72 m; width = 60 − 4 − 4 = 52 m. Inner area = 72 × 52 = 3744 m². Outer area = 80 × 60 = 4800 m². Path area = 4800 − 3744 = 1056 m².
cards.memory_hook: PATH INSIDE: subtract 2w from EACH dimension. 80 − 2(4) = 72; 60 − 2(4) = 52. Then: Outer − Inner = 4800 − 3744 = 1056. PATH OUTSIDE adds 2w. PATH INSIDE subtracts 2w. Same formula, different direction!

cards.front: A circular pond has radius 10 m. A 2 m wide path surrounds it. Find the area of the path. (π = 3.14)
cards.back: Inner radius r = 10 m. Outer radius R = 10 + 2 = 12 m. Path area = π(R² − r²) = π(12² − 10²) = π(144 − 100) = π × 44 = 3.14 × 44 = 138.16 m². Answer: Path area ≈ 138.16 m².
cards.memory_hook: CIRCULAR PATH area = π(R² − r²) = π(outer² − inner²). Outer radius = inner + path width. This is the RING formula — like the area of a ring/washer. Subtract the inner hole from the outer disk!

cards.front: The area of a parallelogram is 150 cm² and its height is 10 cm. Find the base.
cards.back: Area = base × height. 150 = base × 10. Base = 150 ÷ 10 = 15 cm. Answer: Base = 15 cm. This is a REVERSE problem — finding a dimension from the area. Always rearrange the formula: base = Area ÷ height (when area and height are known).
cards.memory_hook: REVERSE FORMULA: if Area = b × h, then b = Area ÷ h and h = Area ÷ b. Triangle: if Area = ½bh, then b = 2×Area÷h. Always rearrange the formula for the unknown. Formula triangles help: draw Area/b×h and cover the unknown!

cards.front: Convert: (a) 2.5 m² to cm² (b) 450,000 cm² to m².
cards.memory_hook: m² TO cm²: MULTIPLY by 10,000 (getting smaller unit = more of them). cm² TO m²: DIVIDE by 10,000 (getting bigger unit = fewer of them). The conversion factor (10,000) comes from 100² — SQUARE the linear conversion!

cards.front: Among all rectangles with the same perimeter, which has the maximum area?
cards.back: The SQUARE has the maximum area among all rectangles with the same perimeter. Example: Perimeter = 40 cm. Rectangle 1: 15×5, area = 75. Rectangle 2: 12×8, area = 96. Rectangle 3: 10×10 (square), area = 100. The square (all sides equal) gives the maximum area for a fixed perimeter. This is why most efficient containers are square/circular in cross-section — they enclose maximum area per unit perimeter.
cards.memory_hook: SQUARE = MOST AREA for given PERIMETER. The more SQUARE a rectangle, the more efficient. The MOST square rectangle IS a square! Nature uses this: circular/square containers waste the least material for the most volume.

cards.front: A garden is shaped like a right-angled triangle with legs 30 m and 40 m. A semicircular flowerbed of diameter 10 m is cut from the hypotenuse side. Find the remaining area.
cards.back: Step 1: Hypotenuse = √(30² + 40²) = √(900+1600) = √2500 = 50 m. Step 2: Triangle area = ½ × 30 × 40 = 600 m². Step 3: Semicircle: diameter = 10 m → radius = 5 m. Area = ½ × π × r² = ½ × 3.14 × 25 = 39.25 m². Step 4: Remaining area = 600 − 39.25 = 560.75 m². This is a COMBINED SHAPES problem — subtract the removed shape from the main shape.
cards.memory_hook: COMBINED SHAPES: find each part's area separately, then add or subtract. Main shape − hole/removed shape = remaining. This appears in every real building plan — rooms subtracted from floors, windows from walls, flowerbeds from gardens!
